source_text: Quam pulchrum spectaculum Deo, quum Christianus cum dolore congreditur, quum adversum minas et supplicia et tormenta componitur; quum strepitum mortis55 et horrorem carnificis irripiens inculcat; quum, libertatem suam adversus reges et principes erigit, soli Deo, cujus est, cedit; quum triumphator et victor, ipsi qui adversum se sententia dixit, stultat ! Vicit enim qui quod contendit obtinuit. Quis non miles sub oculis imperatoris audacius periculum provocet? nemo enim praemium percipit ante experimentum: et imperator tamen, quod non habet, non dat; non potest propagare vitam, potest honestare militiam. At enim Dei miles nec in dolore deseritur, nec morte finitur. Sic Christianus miser videri potest, non potest inveniri. Vos ipsi calamitosos viros fertis ad coelum, Mucium Scaevolam, qui, quum errasset in regem, periisset in hostibus, nisi dexteram perdidisset. Et quot ex nostris non dextram solum, sed totum corpus uri, cremari, sine ullis ejulatibus, pertulerunt, quum dimitti praesertim haberent in sua potestate? Viros cum Mucio, vel cum Aquilio aut Regulo comparo? Pueri et mulierculae nostrae cruces et tormenta, feras et omnes suppliciorum terriculas, inspirata patientia doloris, illudunt. Nec intelligilis, o miseri, neminem esse qui, aut sine ratione velit poenam subire, aut tormenta sine Deo posse sustinere. Nisi forte vos decipit, quod, Deum nescientes, divitiis affluant, honoribus floreant, polleant potestatibus. Miseri! in hoc altius tolluntur, ut decidant altius. Hi enim, ut victimae, ad supplicium saginantur; ut hostiae ad poenam, coronantur. In hoc adeo quidam imperiis ac dominationibus eriguntur, ut ingenium eorum perditae mentis licentiae potestatis libere nundinentur: absque enim notitia Dei, quae potest esse solida felicitas, quum mors sit somnio similis? antequam tenetur, elabitur. Rex es? et tam times quam timeris: et, quamlibet sis multo comitatu stipatus, ad periculum tamen solus es. Dives es? sed fortunae male creditur, et magno viatico breve vitae iter non instruitur, sed oneratur. Fascibus et purpuris gloriaris? vanus error hominis et inanis cultus dignitatis, fulgere purpura, mente sordescere. Nobilitate generosus es? parentes tuos laudas? Omnes tamen pari sorte nascimur; sola virtute distinguimur. Nos igitur qui moribus et pudore censemur, merito malis voluptatibus et pompis vestris et spectaculis abstinemus: quorum et de sacris originem novimus, et noxia blandimenta damnamus. Nam in ludis curulibus, quis non horreat populi in se rixantis insaniam? In gladiatoriis, homicidii disciplinam? In scenicis etiam non minor furore turpitudo prolixior: nunc enim mimus vel exponit adulteria, vel monstrat; nunc enervis histrio amorem dum fingit, infligit. Idem deos vestros, induendo stupra, suspiria, odia, dedecorat. Idem, simulatis doloribus, lacrymas vestras vanis gestibus et nutibus provocat. Sic homicidium in vero flagitatis, in mendacio fletis.
pass_a_gloss: How beautiful a spectacle to God, when a Christian approaches with pain, when he composes himself against threats and punishments and torments; when, snatching away the noise of death and the horror of the executioner, he treads it underfoot; when, raising his freedom against kings and princes, he yields to God alone, whose it is; when, a conqueror and victor, he mocks the one who pronounced a sentence against him. For he has conquered who has obtained what he contended for. Who would not, under the eyes of the emperor, more boldly provoke danger? For no one receives a reward before a test; and the emperor, moreover, does not give what he does not have; he cannot prolong life, but he can honor military service. But a soldier of God is not deserted in pain, nor does he end in death. Thus a Christian can be seen as wretched, but cannot be found to be so. You yourselves carry calamitous men to heaven, Mucius Scaevola, who, when he had erred against the king, would have perished among the enemies, if he had not lost his right hand. And how many of ours have not only endured their right hand being burned, but their whole body, without any lamentations, when they could have been released, especially since it was in their power? Do I compare men with Mucius, or with Aquilius or Regulus? Our boys and little women, inspired by the patience of pain, mock crosses and torments, wild beasts and all the terrors of punishments. And you do not understand, o wretched ones, that there is no one who would undergo punishment without reason, or endure torments without God. Unless perhaps you are deceived by the fact that, not knowing God, you abound in riches, flourish in honors, and are powerful in powers. Wretched ones! They are lifted up the higher, so that they may fall the deeper. For they are fattened like victims for punishment; they are crowned like sacrificial animals for penalty. Indeed, some are elevated to empires and dominions, so that their genius may freely traffic in the licentiousness of a lost mind's power: for without the knowledge of God, what solid happiness can there be, when death is similar to a dream? It slips away before it is grasped. You are a king? And you fear as much as you are feared: and, although you are surrounded by a large retinue, you are alone in danger. You are rich? But fortune is poorly trusted, and a large sum of money does not provide for the brief journey of life, but rather burdens it. Do you glory in fasces and purple? It is a vain error of man and an empty cult of dignity, to shine in purple, to be sordid in mind. Are you noble by birth? Do you praise your parents? Nevertheless, we are all born with an equal fate; we are distinguished only by virtue. We, therefore, who are judged by our morals and shame, rightly abstain from your evil pleasures and pomp and spectacles: for we know the origin of these things from sacred sources, and we condemn their harmful allurements. For in the curule games, who does not shudder at the insanity of the people fighting among themselves? In the gladiatorial games, the discipline of homicide? In the scenic games, too, there is no less turpitude, prolonged in fury: now the mime either exposes adulteries or shows them; now the effeminate actor, while feigning love, inflicts it. The same actor dishonors your gods, by portraying rapes, sighs, hatreds. The same, with simulated pains, provokes your tears with empty gestures and nods. Thus you commit homicide in truth, but weep in falsehood.

choices.why: stultat is a rare verb that means to mock or scorn

choices.english: inspired by the patience of pain
choices.why: the phrase is used to describe the Christian's ability to endure suffering
the phrase is used to describe the vain glory of earthly power
the phrase is used to describe the moral corruption that accompanies earthly power
the phrase is used to describe the corrupting influence of worldly pleasures

pass_b_english: What a magnificent spectacle a Christian offers God when he faces suffering head-on, steeling himself against threats, punishments, and tortures. He snatches away death's terror and the executioner's horror and tramples them underfoot. He asserts his freedom against kings and princes, yet yields to God alone, to whom that freedom belongs. As a conqueror and victor, he mocks the very judge who sentenced him, for the true victor is the one who gains what he strives for.

What soldier would not court danger more boldly under the emperor's gaze? No one receives a reward without being tested, yet the emperor cannot give what he does not possess: he cannot prolong life, only honor military service. But God's soldier is never abandoned in suffering, nor does death finish him. A Christian may look wretched, but he cannot be found wretched.

You yourselves exalt tragic figures to the heavens—Mucius Scaevola, who would have perished at enemy hands after failing to assassinate a king, had he not thrust his own right hand into the fire. And how many of ours have endured not just a hand, but their entire bodies being burned and consumed, without a single cry, even though release was in their power? Do I compare our people with Mucius, or with Aquilius or Regulus? Our boys and young women, strengthened by the patience that suffering inspires, laugh at crosses, torments, wild beasts, and every terror of punishment.

You do not understand, you wretched ones, that no one willingly undergoes punishment without reason, and no one can endure torture without God. Perhaps you are deceived because, in your ignorance of God, you overflow with riches, flourish in honors, and wield great power. Miserable creatures! You are lifted higher only to fall deeper. Like victims fattened for slaughter, like sacrificial beasts crowned for the altar, you are prepared for punishment. Some are raised to empire and dominion so that their genius may freely traffic in the licentiousness of a lost mind's power. Without knowledge of God, what solid happiness can exist when death is like a dream—slipping away before it can be grasped?

Are you a king? You fear as much as you are feared, and despite your vast retinue, you face danger alone. Are you rich? Fortune is a poor credit risk; a massive fortune does not provision life's brief journey—it burdens it. Do you glory in fasces and purple? That is a vain human error and an empty cult of dignity: to shine in purple while the mind grows sordid. Are you noble by birth? Do you praise your parents? We are all born to the same lot; only virtue distinguishes us.

Therefore we, who are judged by our character and our sense of shame, rightly abstain from your wicked pleasures, pomp, and spectacles. We know their sacred origins, and we condemn their harmful allurements. In the curule games, who does not shudder at the insanity of a populace rioting against itself? In the gladiatorial games, you witness the discipline of homicide. In the scenic games, turpitude is no less, only prolonged by fury: now the mime exposes or enacts adulteries; now the effeminate actor, while feigning love, inflicts it. The same performer dishonors your gods by portraying rapes, sighs, and hatreds. With simulated pains, he provokes your tears through empty gestures and nods. Thus you commit homicide in truth, but weep in falsehood.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful clause-by-clause translation, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that preserves all nuances, including the specific historical reference to Mucius Scaevola and the rhetorical questions regarding kings and the wealthy. All theological and moral distinctions are maintained.
